content.text: Electricity is one of the most versatile forms of energy. It can be converted into heat, light, sound, kinetic energy, and many other forms with high efficiency. But electrical energy is not free — we pay for the energy our appliances use. Understanding how to calculate electrical energy and power is essential for designing safe and efficient electrical systems, selecting the right components, and making sense of electricity bills.

In this lesson, we will explore the equations for electrical energy and power, learn about the kilowatt-hour as a practical unit of energy, calculate electricity costs, and understand the safety devices that protect us from the dangers of electrical faults.

When charge flows through a component, electrical energy is transferred to other forms. The amount of energy transferred depends on three things: the potential difference across the component, the current through it, and the time for which the current flows.
The energy transferred by an electrical component is given by:

(green and yellow striped in the UK) is a safety feature in mains electrical systems. It connects the metal casing of an appliance to the ground (earth).
If a live wire comes loose inside an appliance and touches the metal casing, the casing becomes live.
The earth wire provides a low-resistance path from the casing to the ground.
A large current flows through the earth wire, which causes the fuse to blow (or the circuit breaker to trip), cutting off the electricity supply.
This prevents anyone who touches the casing from receiving a dangerous electric shock.
Without the earth wire, the metal casing could remain live, and anyone touching it could receive a fatal electric shock, as the current would flow through their body to the ground.

"A higher-wattage appliance always costs more to run."
Cost depends on energy used, which is power multiplied by time. A 3 kW kettle used for 5 minutes costs less than a 100 W lamp left on for 24 hours.
"The fuse rating should match the current exactly."
the normal operating current. If it matched exactly, normal fluctuations could blow the fuse. But it should not be too far above, or it would fail to protect against faults.
"The earth wire carries current during normal operation."
Under normal conditions, no current flows through the earth wire. It only carries current when there is a fault (such as a live wire touching the metal casing).
"Double insulation means double the amount of insulation material."
Double insulation means there are two independent layers of insulation between live parts and the user. It does not necessarily mean twice the thickness.

Explain why the fuse is placed in the live wire.

The fuse is in the live wire because the live wire is at high voltage (alternating around 230 V). If the fuse is in the live wire and it blows, the appliance is disconnected from the high-voltage supply, making it safe to touch. If the fuse were in the neutral wire instead, even after it blows, the live wire would still be connected to the appliance, and the metal casing (in a fault) could still be at 230 V — posing a lethal shock risk.

Explain the purpose of the earth wire and what happens during a fault.

The earth wire connects the metal casing of the appliance to the ground. If a live wire becomes loose and touches the metal casing, a large current flows through the casing, along the earth wire to ground (because the earth wire has very low resistance). This large current causes the fuse to blow (or the circuit breaker to trip), disconnecting the appliance from the mains supply. Without the earth wire, the casing would remain live and anyone touching it could receive a fatal electric shock.
